scout.purpose: Responsive constraints and generated binding types make View screens maintainable without manual lookup or unsafe global references.
scout.realWorldUse: ConstraintLayout expresses relationships in one hierarchy, while View Binding generates a binding class for each eligible XML layout.
scout.outcome: Create a fully constrained layout, understand 0dp match-constraints, and own a binding only for the corresponding view lifecycle.

sections.title: Each axis needs a resolvable position and size

blocks.text: ConstraintLayout positions children through relationships to the parent or other views. A child normally needs sufficient horizontal and vertical constraints; design-editor coordinates are not runtime constraints. A dimension of 0dp means match constraints, allowing opposing constraints to determine size. Chains distribute groups, barriers follow the most extreme referenced edge, and guidelines provide percentage or fixed anchors. Prefer a small number of meaningful relationships over recreating nested rows mechanically. Circular or ambiguous constraints may produce unexpected positions or warnings, so inspect the blueprint and run at varied widths.

blocks.caption: Opposing constraints and 0dp allow the editor to fill the remaining bounded region.

sections.title: Generated binding replaces manual ID lookup

blocks.text: Enabling View Binding generates a class from each module layout. Inflating or binding the correct layout returns typed properties for views with IDs, catching many mismatches at compile time and removing casts. It is different from Data Binding: View Binding performs no expression evaluation or observable binding language. A binding does not own lifecycle or state; it merely references the inflated views. Include and merge layouts affect generated shapes, and layouts with configuration alternatives must expose compatible IDs and types so one binding API remains valid.

blocks.caption: The activity binding remains valid for the activity view lifetime and exposes typed child references.

sections.title: A binding must not outlive its hierarchy

blocks.text: An activity binding typically lives as long as that activity instance’s content view. A fragment object can outlive its view between onDestroyView and a later onCreateView, so fragment binding must be cleared when the view is destroyed. Access it only while the view lifecycle is valid. Do not put binding in ViewModel, repository, singleton, adapter data, or asynchronous callbacks that can outlive the view. Render immutable state into views and unregister listeners or collectors with the view lifecycle. A binding leak is still a View leak even though the property is type-safe.

blocks.caption: The fragment releases references when its view hierarchy ends while the fragment instance may remain.

blocks.title: Type-safe is not lifecycle-safe
blocks.text: Generated references prevent lookup casts but cannot stop an owner retaining destroyed views.

trap_check.mistake: Trusting editor positions without runtime constraints.
trap_check.why: Design-time coordinates are not sufficient layout rules.
trap_check.fix: Constrain both axes and test multiple dimensions.

trap_check.mistake: Keeping fragment binding until fragment destruction.
trap_check.why: The fragment often outlives its view and retains the old hierarchy.

challenge_intro.task: Convert a nested note editor to ConstraintLayout and View Binding, then prove the binding is unavailable after onDestroyView.
challenge_intro.successLooksLike: Both axes are fully constrained at narrow and wide sizes. No findViewById or unsafe global view reference remains. View lifecycle collection and binding cleanup are demonstrated.
